clinicalPearls: TAFRO is an acronym for Thrombocytopenia, Anasarca (oedema, ascites and effusions), Fever, Reticulin fibrosis of the marrow (with Renal dysfunction) and Organomegaly.

It is regarded as a distinct, aggressive clinical subtype within the spectrum of HHV-8-negative idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (iMCD-TAFRO), although some cases do not fully meet Castleman criteria.

It is distinguished from other idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease by thrombocytopenia rather than thrombocytosis, severe anasarca, only mild lymphadenopathy and relatively preserved immunoglobulins instead of marked hypergammaglobulinaemia.
The clinical picture is driven by a cytokine storm, especially interleukin-6 and vascular endothelial growth factor, causing systemic inflammation and vascular hyperpermeability.
Lymph node histology resembles hyaline-vascular or mixed Castleman disease with atretic germinal centres, while the bone marrow shows megakaryocytic hyperplasia and reticulin fibrosis.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion — infection (HHV-8, HIV, EBV), malignancy (especially lymphoma), autoimmune disease and POEMS syndrome must be ruled out.
Presentation is often acute with rapidly progressive renal impairment and effusions, and the syndrome can be life-threatening.

Treatment mainstays include corticosteroids and anti-interleukin-6 therapy (for example tocilizumab or siltuximab), with rituximab, ciclosporin or intensive immunosuppression reserved for refractory or critically ill patients.
reference.pathophysiology: TAFRO syndrome is a systemic hyperinflammatory disorder thought to arise from dysregulated cytokine production, in which interleukin-6 and vascular endothelial growth factor play central roles. Excess interleukin-6 drives fever, an acute-phase response and reactive changes in lymphoid tissue and marrow, while vascular endothelial growth factor increases vascular permeability, producing the striking anasarca with ascites and pleural effusions that characterises the condition. Platelet consumption together with marrow megakaryocytic hyperplasia and reticulin fibrosis contributes to thrombocytopenia, and microvascular and immune-mediated injury underlie the frequent renal dysfunction. The initiating trigger is unknown, with autoimmune and antigenic or viral stimuli postulated, but by definition recognised causes such as HHV-8 infection are absent. The syndrome overlaps with idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease, sharing reactive lymph node histology with atretic germinal centres, yet it is set apart clinically by thrombocytopenia, severe fluid overload, comparatively small lymph nodes and the absence of marked hypergammaglobulinaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease, non-TAFRO/plasma cell type
Autoimmune disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, adult-onset Still's disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count (thrombocytopenia, anaemia) with a blood film
Inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein) alongside interleukin-6 and vascular endothelial growth factor levels
Cross-sectional imaging for effusions, ascites, organomegaly and lymphadenopathy
Excisional lymph node biopsy for histology
Bone marrow examination (megakaryocytic hyperplasia and reticulin fibrosis)
Exclusion work-up including HHV-8 and HIV testing, autoimmune serology, and serum immunoglobulins with free light chains to exclude POEMS
redFlags: Rapidly progressive renal failure requiring renal replacement therapy
Refractory anasarca with large effusions and respiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: TAFRO syndrome is more acute and aggressive than classic idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease and can be fatal from multi-organ failure. Timely immunosuppression and anti-interleukin-6 therapy nonetheless induce remission in a substantial proportion of patients.
pitfalls: Attributing isolated thrombocytopenia to immune thrombocytopenia and missing the wider systemic syndrome.
Delaying the lymph node or bone marrow biopsy needed to establish the diagnosis.
Failing to exclude HHV-8 and HIV, which would change classification and management.
Confusing it with POEMS syndrome or an autoimmune connective tissue disease.
Underestimating severity given the potential for rapid multi-organ deterioration.
references: International consensus diagnostic and treatment guidelines for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease
management: High-dose corticosteroids as first-line immunosuppression to dampen the cytokine storm
Anti-interleukin-6 therapy with tocilizumab or siltuximab targeting the central driver cytokine
Escalation to ciclosporin, rituximab or cytotoxic chemotherapy in corticosteroid-refractory or severe disease
Supportive care for anasarca, renal dysfunction including renal replacement therapy, and thrombocytopenia with platelet support as needed
Intensive organ support for multi-organ failure in critically ill patients
Rigorous exclusion of infection, lymphoma, autoimmune disease and POEMS syndrome, which is integral to the diagnosis
Monitoring of platelets, inflammatory markers, interleukin-6 and renal function to track response
Multidisciplinary haematology-led care with critical care support
